'''Janina Hosiasson-Lindenbaum''' (December 5, 1899{{mdash}}April 1942) was a Polish logician and philosopher. She published some twenty research papers along with translations into Polish of three books by [[Bertrand Russell]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last1=Zygmunt|first1=Jan|last2=Purdy|first2=Robert|date=2014-12-01|orig-year=2014|title=Adolf Lindenbaum: Notes on his Life, with Bibliography and Selected References|journal=Logica Universalis|language=en|volume=8|issue=3–4|pages=285–320|doi=10.1007/s11787-014-0108-2|issn=1661-8297|doi-access=free}}</ref> The main focus of her writings was on foundational problems related to probability, induction and confirmation.<ref name=":3">{{Cite book|title=European philosophy of science-- Philosophy of science in Europe and the Viennese Heritage|publisher=Springer International Publishing|editor1-last=Galavotti|editor1-first=Maria Carla|editor1-link= Maria Carla Galavotti|editor2-last= Nemeth|editor2-first= Elisabeth|editor3-last=Stadler|editor3-first= Friedrich|isbn=9783319018997|location=Cham|pages=78–81|chapter=Janina Hosiasson (1899 -1942)|oclc=857813353|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=UE_CBAAAQBAJ&dq=%22Janina+Hosiasson+%281899+-1942%29%22+++&pg=PA7|date = 2013-08-28}}</ref> She is noted especially for authoring the first printed discussion of the [[Raven paradox|Raven Paradox]]<ref name=":1">{{Cite book|title=Women in mathematics : celebrating the centennial of the Mathematical Association of America|isbn=9783319666945|location=Cham, Switzerland|pages=76–77|chapter=Janina Hosiasson-Lindenbaum (1899-1942)|oclc=1015215187|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=eDVBDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA76|last1 = Beery|first1 = Janet L.|author1-link= Janet Beery |last2=Greenwald|first2=Sarah J.|last3=Jensen-Vallin|first3=Jacqueline A.|author3-link=Jacqueline Jensen-Vallin|last4=Mast|first4=Maura B.|author4-link=Maura Mast|date=2017-12-02}}</ref> which she credits to [[Carl Hempel]]<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Vranas|first=P. B. M.|date=2004-09-01|title=Hempel's Raven Paradox: A Lacuna in the Standard Bayesian Solution|journal=The British Journal for the Philosophy of Science|language=en|volume=55|issue=3|pages=546|doi=10.1093/bjps/55.3.545|s2cid=14761025|issn=0007-0882|quote=The exact origin of Hempel's paradox is shrouded in mystery. Although Hempel apparently did not formulate the paradox in print until 1943 ([1943], p. 128), Hosiasson-Lindenbaum formulated it as early as 1940 ([1940], p. 136): she attributed it to Hempel but gave no reference. (Hempel ([1945], p. 21 n. 2) referred to 'discussions' with her.) The paradox was 'foreshadowed' (Jeffrey [1995], p. 3) but by no means formulated by Hempel in 1937 ([1937), p. 222).|url=https://philpapers.org/archive/VRAHRP.pdf}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Hosiasson-Lindenbaum|first=Janina|date=1940|title=On Confirmation|jstor=2268173|journal=The Journal of Symbolic Logic|volume=5|issue=4|pages=133–148|doi=10.2307/2268173|s2cid=195347283 }}</ref> and the probabilistic solution she outlined to it.<ref name=":3" />  Shot by the Gestapo in 1942,<ref name=":0" /> she, like her husband [[Adolf Lindenbaum]], and many other eminent representatives of Polish logic, shared the fate of millions of Jews murdered on Polish soil by the Nazis.<ref>{{Citation|last=Wójcicki|first=Ryszard|chapter=The Postwar Panorama of Logic in Poland|date=1997|chapter-url=https://doi.org/10.1007/978-94-017-0487-8_28|title=Logic and Scientific Methods: Volume One of the Tenth International Congress of Logic, Methodology and Philosophy of Science, Florence, August 1995|pages=499|editor-last=Dalla Chiara|editor-first=Maria Luisa|series=Synthese Library|place=Dordrecht|publisher=Springer Netherlands|language=en|doi=10.1007/978-94-017-0487-8_28|isbn=978-94-017-0487-8|quote=Such eminent representatives of Polish logic as [[Adolf Lindenbaum]], his wife Janina Hossasion Lindenbaum, Mojiesz Presburger, Józef Pepis, Jan Salamucha, Z. Schmierer, Mordchaj Wajsberg shared the fate of millions of Jews murdered on Polish soil by Nazi's occupants.|access-date=2021-02-26|editor2-last=Doets|editor2-first=Kees|editor3-last=Mundici|editor3-first=Daniele|editor4-last=van Benthem|editor4-first=Johan|chapter-url-access=subscription}}</ref>

== Biography ==
Janina Hosiasson was born on 6 December 1899 in Warsaw, the daughter of the merchant Josef Hosiasson and his wife Sophia Feigenblat.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://szukajwarchiwach.pl/72/200/0/-/126/skan/full/ucIIlcq3FqfFhN1eaOExyw |title=Birth record of Yanina Hosiasson |access-date=2018-04-16 |archive-date=2018-04-16 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180416074850/http://szukajwarchiwach.pl/72/200/0/-/126/skan/full/ucIIlcq3FqfFhN1eaOExyw |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref name=":0" />

She was a student of [[Tadeusz Kotarbinski]] and [[Jan Łukasiewicz]] at the [[University of Warsaw]] and received her doctorate there under Kotarbinski in 1926<ref name=":0" /> with a dissertation on the "Justification of Inductive Reasoning".<ref name=":3" /> She would then combine her continuing research with employment as a teacher of philosophy in a secondary school.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Polish philosophers of science and nature in the 20th century|date=2001|publisher=Rodopi|others=Krajewski, Władysław.|isbn=9042014970|location=Amsterdam|pages=97|chapter=Janina Hosiasson-Lindenbaumowa: the logic of induction / Anna Jedynak|oclc=50325256|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=TR93KttgkyoC&dq=janina+Hosiasson-Lindenbaum+Owa&pg=PA97}}</ref> By the late 1920s she was a respected philosopher of logic of the [[Lwów–Warsaw school]] who actively participated in the second Polish Philosophical Congress held in Warsaw in September 1927 and (like her husband-to-be) delivered papers at the First Congress of Mathematicians from Slavic Countries held in Warsaw and [[Poznań]] in September 1929.<ref name=":0" /> Janina then went, on a scholarship from the Polish Ministry of Religious Affairs and Public Education, to spend the 1929/30 academic year studying philosophy in Cambridge.<ref name=":0" />

In 1935, Hosiasson became the first woman to have work published in the journal ''[[Erkenntnis]]''.<ref name=":7">{{Cite journal |last=Sznajder |first=Marta |date=2022-07-17 |title=Janina Hosiasson-Lindenbaum on Analogical Reasoning: New Sources |url=https://pure.rug.nl/ws/files/1095676396/s10670-022-00586-y.pdf |journal=Erkenntnis |language=en |volume=89 |issue=4 |at=1 Hosiasson’s Work in the 1940s |doi=10.1007/s10670-022-00586-y |issn=1572-8420 |doi-access=free}}</ref> She was one of the speakers at the first Unity of Science Congress in Paris 1935.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Galavotti|first=Maria Carla|author-link= Maria Carla Galavotti |date=2018-10-25|title=The Sessions on Induction and Probability at the 1935 Paris Congress: An overview|url=http://journals.openedition.org/philosophiascientiae/1629|journal=Philosophia Scientiæ. Travaux d'histoire et de philosophie des sciences|language=en|issue=22–3|pages=213–232|doi=10.4000/philosophiascientiae.1629|issn=1281-2463|quote=The First International Congress for the Unity of Science (Congrès international de philosophie scientifique) held in Paris in 1935 hosted two sessions devoted to “Induction” and “Probability” respectively. Outstanding representatives of the movement for scientific philosophy read papers in those sessions: the one on Induction hosted papers by Hans Reichenbach, Moritz Schlick, and Rudolf Carnap, while the one on Probability hosted papers by Reichenbach, Bruno de Finetti, Zygmunt Zawirski, Schlick, and Janina Hosiasson..|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|last=Wolters|first=Gereon|title="Wrongful life" reloaded: Logical empiricism's philosophy of biology 1934-1936 (Prague/Paris/Copenhagen): With historical and political intermezzos (2018)|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/326589082|website=ResearchGate}}</ref> She is also known to have participated in the preliminary meeting for the same in Prague the previous year.<ref name=":5" /><ref name=":6" /> On December 18, 1935, Janina Hosiasson married mathematician and logician Adolf Lindenbaum in [[Wąbrzeźno]], Pomerania. (The marriage certificate is located in the National Archives in Toruń, Poland.).<ref name=":4" /> The couple would then reside together in the [[Żoliborz|Zoliborz]] district of Warsaw.<ref name=":0" /> After marriage Janina would use the surname Hosiasson-Lindenbaum.<ref name=":2">{{Cite book|title=Alfred Tarski : early work in Poland : geometry and teaching|last1=McFarland|first1=Andrew|last2=McFarland|first2=Joanna|last3=Smith|first3=James T.|date=2014-08-11|others=McFarland, Andrew,, McFarland, Joanna,, Smith, James T.|isbn=9781493914746|location=New York|pages=335|chapter=p.335|oclc=888074959|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=olNDBAAAQBAJ&dq=Janina+Hosiasson-Lindenbaumowa&pg=PA335}}</ref> She attended the second Unity of Science Congress held in Copenhagen in 1936<ref name=":6">{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=NEztCAAAQBAJ&q=Janina+Hosiasson|title=The Vienna Circle and the Lvov-Warsaw School|isbn=9789400928299|editor-last=Szaniawski|editor-first=Klemens|pages=1, 444|date=2012-12-06|publisher=Springer }}</ref> and had also (like [[Alfred Tarski]]) been scheduled to present her research at the fifth Unity of Science Congress at [[Harvard University|Harvard]] in September 1939.<ref name=":2" /> Fatefully, however, she was unable to sail in time<ref name=":2" />—she applied for passage on the next boat to America after that taken by Tarski but her visa was denied.<ref name=":5">{{Cite book|title=Alfred Tarski : life and logic|last1=Burdman Feferman|first1=Anita|author1-link=Anita Burdman Feferman|date=2004|publisher=Cambridge University Press|last2=Feferman|first2=Solomon|author2-link=Solomon Feferman|isbn=9780521802406|location=Cambridge, UK|pages=[https://archive.org/details/alfredtarskilife0000fefe/page/108 108]|oclc=54691904|url=https://archive.org/details/alfredtarskilife0000fefe/page/108}}</ref>

On 1 September, Germany invaded Poland. On 6 September 1939, with Warsaw under artillery fire, the couple fled the city on foot.<ref name=":4">{{Citation|last1=Purdy|first1=Robert|chapter=Adolf Lindenbaum, Metric Spaces and Decompositions|date=2018|title=The Lvov-Warsaw School. Past and Present|pages=505–550|editor-last=Garrido|editor-first=Ángel|series=Studies in Universal Logic|publisher=Springer International Publishing|language=en|doi=10.1007/978-3-319-65430-0_36|isbn=9783319654300|last2=Zygmunt|first2=Jan|editor2-last=Wybraniec-Skardowska|editor2-first=Urszula|editor2-link=Urszula Wybraniec-Skardowska}}</ref> As Janina would report in letters to [[Otto Neurath]] and [[G. E. Moore|G.E. Moore]],<ref>[https://www.fn.uw.edu.pl/index.php/fn/article/view/886/1174 JANINA HOSIASSON-LINDENBAUM’S LETTER TO GEORGE EDWARD MOORE] (Appendix to) Szubka, T. (2018). [[doi:10.14394/filnau.2018.0007|"List Janiny Hosiasson-Lindenbaum do George’a Edwarda Moore’a."]] ''Filozofia Nauki'', ''26''(1), 129-141.</ref> their progress east was slow and the road repeatedly strafed by the [[Luftwaffe]].<ref name=":4" /> The couple became separated after Janina accepted a lift on a motorcycle to [[Rivne]].<ref name=":4" /> From there, she made her way to [[Vilnius]] where she eventually learnt her husband had taken refuge in [[Białystok|Bialystok]].<ref name=":4" /> Soviet forces entered Poland on 17 September and both cities would fall under Russian occupation within the same month.<ref name=":4" /> Janina later met her husband in Bialystok but, disagreeing about where best to survive, he chose to remain there whilst she returned to Vilnius (a city under Polish jurisdiction at the outbreak of war but which the occupying Soviets formally returned to a then notionally independent [[Lithuania]]).<ref name=":4" />

On 22 June 22, 1941, Germany invaded (the Polish territories annexed by) the Soviet Union and within days, their troops had entered Bialystok and, soon after, Vilnius.<ref name=":0" /> At some point before July 1941 Adolf Lindenbaum moved to Vilnius, staying in a small satellite community in the east of the city'''.'''<ref name=":4" /> At some point before the middle of August 1941, Adolf, along with his sister Stefanja, would be arrested and then, in nearby [[Naujoji Vilnia]], shot by German forces or their Lithuanian collaborators.<ref name=":4" />

Hosiasson was arrested soon after the Nazis took over Vilnius and, from October 1941, was held in [[Lukiškės Prison]]. Marta Sznajder suggests she was likely shot on 29 March 1942.<ref name=":7" />

== Select works ==
*  [https://www.jstor.org/stable/2268173 "On Confirmation"], ''[[Journal of Symbolic Logic]]'', Vol. 5, No. 4 (Dec., 1940), pp.&nbsp;133–148.<ref>Free to read online at [[JSTOR]] with registration - [https://www.jstor.org/stable/2266658 short review] by [[Saunders Mac Lane|MacLane, Saunders]] (June 1941). similarly available with JSTOR registration and also available for [https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-symbolic-logic/article/abs/janina-hosiassonlindenbaum-on-confirmation-the-journal-of-symbolic-logic-vol-5-1940-pp-133148/FCD2FFE0F4BC666F595F7860967E7E9B full preview] via [[Cambridge University Press#Digital developments|Cambridge Core]]</ref>
*  [https://doi.org/10.1093/mind/XL.157.23 "Why do we prefer probabilities relative to many data?"] ''[[Mind (journal)|Mind]]'', Volume XL, Issue 157, (Jan, 1931), pp.&nbsp;23–36
* "[https://doi.org/10.1093/mind/L.200.351 Induction et Analogie: Comparison de leur fondement]", ''[[Mind (journal)|Mind]]'', Vol L, Issue 200, (Oct, 1941), pp.&nbsp;351–365
*  [https://www.jstor.org/stable/20114053 "Theoretical Aspects of the Advancement of Knowledge"], ''[[Synthese]]'', Vol. 7, No. 4/5 (1948/49), pp.&nbsp;253–261.
A complete listing of Hosiasson's published works has made available by Marta Sznajder.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-05-04 |title=Hosiassion Bibliography |url=https://martasznajder.com/hosiassion-bibliography/ |access-date=2024-02-04 |website=Marta Sznajder |language=en}}</ref>
